title: Brent near $94; Oil extends rally as fresh attacks raise fears of Gulf supply disruptions - CNBC TV18
html:
Brent trades near $94 a barrel and WTI hovers around $84 as attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, reported mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and new shipping restrictions near UAE export hubs revive supply concerns. The gains come despite rising US crude inventories and expectations of a global oil surplus.

Oil extended its two-day rally on Thursday, November 26, as escalating hostilities in West Asia seemed to have raised fresh doubts over the recovery in the region's crude exports.

Brent settled just under $95 a barrel on Wednesday and traded at $94.20 in early Asian hours, having briefly slipped below $90 before bouncing back in this week's trade. West Texas Intermediate hovered near $84 after gaining more than 4% across the previous two sessions.

Several factors are driving the rebound, including attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran backed Houthi militants, with Ras Tanura, the country's main oil export hub, being among their main targets.

Also Read: Yemen's Houthis threaten to target Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports

Iran has also claimed that several vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz struck mines. On Wednesday, the country's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two tankers hit naval mines, exploded and caught fire after they tried to use an unauthorised route as per a Reuters report.

Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia then announced that the military had deployed new systems and upgraded existing ones to tighten surveillance and control of the strait, warning that ships passing without coordinating with Iranian forces had faced greater risks, the report said.

The United Arab Emirates has added to the nervousness as tankers carrying crude, oil products, liquefied gases and chemicals now face restrictions on entering waters near some of the country's main export hubs, according to a Bloomberg report.

A notice covers areas under the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's Petroleum Ports Authority, including waters near the Ruwais refinery complex and loading terminals such as Das Island, and bars vessels unless they call at, or conduct approved business with, ADNOC-PPA facilities, the report noted.

The waters beyond Hormuz have served as the main site for ship-to-ship transfers in the shuttle trade that has supported exports during the war.

Diplomacy has so far brought little relief, though as Tehran has told Washington it would not restore normal shipping through Hormuz until its demands were met, including an end to the US naval blockade of its ports and to the war on all fronts.

Through Qatari mediators, it has offered to reopen the waterway within 48 hours of Washington meeting those conditions. Washington, meanwhile, wants concessions on Iran's nuclear programme, and Tehran also seeks sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets.

Iran's first vice president, Mohammad Reza Aref, said on Wednesday that Tehran was unconcerned about the blockade, which the US reimposed in July, because cargo flows through other borders had risen significantly as per a Reuters report.

He said strategic reserves were strong, and that the government aimed to hold basic goods prices steady for at least three months. Iran still faces one of its sharpest inflation surges in decades, with food prices climbing fastest.

Even so, the rally follows a steep monthly fall. Brent tumbled this month as crude shipments from the Gulf region revived, and the International Energy Agency expects a market surplus this quarter.

Also Read: JD Vance, Marco Rubio meet with Qatari PM as uncertainty mounts over Trump's intentions with Iran

US President Donald Trump also held off on renewed strikes on Iran after the Democrats swept the US midterm elections, which cooled the market further.

US data released on Wednesday showed crude inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels last week, with gasoline and distillate stockpiles also growing, while crude exports fell to their lowest since early August amid higher freight costs and weaker Asian demand.
